The Partition of India. In nineteen forty-seven, the British Indian subcontinent was split into independent India and Pakistan along religious lines, a geopolitical and humanitarian catastrophe. Conceived as a solution to majority-Muslim and majority-Hindu regions, the partition instead triggered mass migration, communal violence, and between two hundred thousand and two million deaths, redefined South Asian geopolitics, and remains a source of tension and trauma across the region.

The partition was announced on August fifteenth, nineteen forty-seven, as British rule ended. India and Pakistan became independent nations that same day, with Mountbatten's Plan proposing the division. Muhammad Ali Jinnah led the Indian National Muslim League's demand for Pakistan, arguing that Muslims needed their own nation-state separate from Hindu-majority India. Mahatma Gandhi opposed partition, advocating instead for a unified independent India with safeguards for religious minorities. His assassination just months later was by a Hindu extremist opposed to his pluralism.

The partition created Pakistan in two geographically separated regions: West Pakistan and East Pakistan, which later became Bangladesh in nineteen seventy-one after civil war and Indian military intervention. Approximately fifteen million people were displaced as Hindus and Sikhs fled Pakistan and Muslims fled India; entire communities were uprooted within weeks, creating refugee camps and humanitarian crises. Communal violence and massacres accompanied the partition, with the Rawalpindi Massacre and violence in Delhi and Punjab among the deadliest, as communities turned against neighbors. The partition left the disputed territory of Kashmir unresolved, leading to three wars between India and Pakistan and ongoing tensions that persist into the twenty-first century. The borders drawn by British administrator Radcliffe, who had never visited India, separated families, severed economic ties, and created lasting resentments and geopolitical instability that fundamentally reshaped South Asia.
